prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

An elevator arrangement has a car displaceable within an elevator shaft between building floors, an elevator control and a fixture located at each floors and connected to the elevator control for an exchange of information. Each fixture includes a sound detector detecting sound propagating within the shaft. The arrangement performs a fixture position learning procedure by determining position information for each fixture based on sound characteristics detected by the sound detector and storing the determined position information for subsequent identification of each of the fixtures. Changes in sound characteristics are detected while the car is displaced through the shaft. Time-dependent occurrences of sound pressure peaks or frequency shifts due to Doppler effects are measured at the fixtures and fixture position information is derived from a sequence order of such occurrences or, alternatively, by correlating the occurrence of sound characteristic changes with current car position information provided by the elevator control.

An elevator arrangement includes a movable elevator car that travels within an elevator shaft, an elevator control system, and a plurality of fixtures arranged at respective floors. The fixtures are connected to the elevator control system so that information can be exchanged between each fixture and the control. These fixtures may be, for example, landing call fixtures, display units, or other floor-associated devices used in the operation of the elevator system.

Each floor fixture is provided with a sound detector configured to detect sound propagating within the elevator shaft. The sound may be produced naturally during elevator operation, generated by movement of the elevator car, or emitted by a dedicated sound source associated with the elevator system. As the elevator car moves through the shaft, the sound detected at different floor fixtures changes in a manner that depends on the relative position of the car and the respective fixture.

The elevator system is configured to carry out a fixture position learning procedure. During this procedure, the system determines position information for each floor fixture and stores that information, for example in the elevator control system or in memory associated with the fixtures. The stored position information enables the elevator control to identify the physical location of each fixture in the shaft or to associate each fixture with a corresponding floor.

The position of each fixture is derived from changes in detected sound characteristics while the elevator car moves through the shaft. For example, as the car passes a fixture, the sound pressure detected by the sound detector may exhibit a characteristic peak or other recognizable change. By evaluating the order or sequence of such sound pressure peaks detected by the fixtures, the system can determine the relative positions of the fixtures along the elevator shaft.

Alternatively or additionally, the system may use Doppler frequency shifts in the detected sound. As the elevator car approaches or moves away from a fixture, the frequency of sound received at the fixture may shift in a way that indicates the relative movement between the car and the fixture. These frequency shifts can be analyzed to determine when the car passes the fixture and, consequently, to determine the fixture’s position.

In another implementation, detected sound changes are correlated with current elevator car position data. The elevator control may already know or estimate the position of the car during travel, for example from an encoder, position sensor, or drive control data. When a sound detector at a fixture detects a characteristic change in sound, the system associates that event with the current car position. The resulting position value is then stored as the position information for that fixture.

In this way, the elevator arrangement can automatically learn the positions of floor fixtures without requiring manual configuration of each fixture location. The use of sound detected within the elevator shaft provides a practical mechanism for identifying fixture positions during installation, commissioning, maintenance, or recalibration of the elevator system.
outputs.L4:
An elevator system can automatically learn and store the positions of floor fixtures located along an elevator hoistway by using sound-based detection. Each floor fixture, such as a landing call device, indicator, communication unit, or other shaft-side component, is equipped with or connected to a sound detector. As the elevator car travels through the shaft, it produces characteristic acoustic effects, including changes in sound pressure, airflow noise, mechanical noise, and frequency shifts caused by relative motion between the car and the fixture.

During a learning or commissioning operation, the elevator car is moved through the hoistway while the sound detectors in the fixtures monitor the acoustic environment. When the car approaches, passes, and moves away from a fixture, the sound detected at that fixture changes in a recognizable way. For example, the detector may register a peak in sound pressure when the car is closest to the fixture. Alternatively, the detector may detect a change in frequency associated with the Doppler effect, where the apparent frequency of sound changes depending on whether the car is moving toward or away from the detector.

The elevator control system receives the acoustic detection data from the fixtures and compares it with car position information obtained from the elevator drive, encoder, position sensor, or another car position measuring device. By determining the order in which the fixtures detect sound pressure peaks, or by measuring the timing of these peaks relative to known car positions, the control system can determine where each fixture is located along the hoistway. In another implementation, the system may analyze Doppler-related frequency changes to identify the moment at which the car passes a fixture and then associate that moment with the corresponding car position.

Once the position of each fixture has been determined, the elevator controller stores this information in memory. The stored data may include the identity of the fixture, the floor or landing associated with the fixture, its vertical position in the shaft, and any communication address or control assignment required for operation. This allows the elevator system to establish a reliable mapping between physical fixture locations and their logical control functions.

After the learning process is complete, the stored position information can be used for normal elevator operation. The controller can accurately communicate with the correct fixture, associate landing calls with the proper floor, verify fixture installation, detect wiring or addressing errors, and support maintenance or diagnostic functions. Because the fixture positions are learned automatically using acoustic measurements, the system can reduce manual configuration work, simplify installation, and improve reliability when fixtures are replaced, added, or serviced.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain an elevator arrangement where fixtures at each floor determine their shaft position from acoustic characteristics detected while the elevator car travels.
counterfactuals.output:
An elevator arrangement of this kind uses sound produced or carried by the moving elevator car to allow floor fixtures to identify where they are located along the hoistway, without requiring each fixture to be manually programmed with its floor number or shaft position.

In general, the system includes:

- An elevator car traveling in a shaft or hoistway.
- Fixtures installed at individual landings, such as hall call panels, landing indicators, door-zone devices, or other floor-mounted electronic units.
- An acoustic sensor in each fixture, for example a microphone or vibration/acoustic pickup.
- A controller or processing unit associated with each fixture or with the elevator system.

As the elevator car moves through the shaft, it produces characteristic acoustic signals. These may come from the car itself, the guide shoes, rollers, door equipment, ventilation, drive components, or from a deliberate acoustic transmitter mounted on the car. The sound field at each landing changes as the car approaches, passes, and moves away.

Each floor fixture listens to the acoustic characteristics detected during car travel. The detected acoustic information may include, for example:

- The time at which the sound level rises and falls.
- The point of maximum acoustic intensity as the car passes the fixture.
- Frequency content or spectral patterns.
- Doppler-related changes.
- Reflections or resonance behavior in the shaft.
- A coded acoustic signal emitted by the car.
- The time relationship between detected sound and known car movement data.

By comparing the detected acoustic pattern with the elevator car’s known travel information, the fixture can determine its position in the shaft. For example, if the elevator controller knows the car position over time, and a particular fixture detects the strongest acoustic event at a specific time, the fixture can associate that event with the car’s known position at that moment. The fixture can then conclude: “I am located at the landing corresponding to this car position.”

A simplified example is:

1. The elevator car performs a learning run through the shaft.
2. Each landing fixture monitors acoustic signals while the car travels.
3. When the car passes a fixture, that fixture detects a distinctive acoustic peak or signature.
4. The elevator controller correlates the time of that detection with the car’s known shaft position.
5. The fixture is assigned its corresponding floor or shaft location automatically.

This arrangement can be useful because it reduces installation and commissioning effort. Instead of manually setting switches, entering floor numbers, or wiring each fixture to a unique address, the fixtures can automatically learn their positions based on acoustic observations during elevator movement.

The method may also be used for verification or diagnostics. If a fixture later detects acoustic events inconsistent with its stored position, the system may identify a configuration error, fixture replacement, wiring mix-up, or possible sensor fault.

In short, the arrangement uses the elevator car as a moving acoustic reference. Fixtures at the floors listen to the sound characteristics generated as the car passes and use those characteristics, often in combination with known car position data, to determine their own shaft positions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a technical description of a fixture position learning procedure for elevator floor fixtures connected to an elevator control, based on detected sound peaks or frequency shifts.
counterfactuals.output:
A fixture position learning procedure can be used to automatically associate elevator floor fixtures, such as hall call buttons, landing displays, lanterns, destination input devices, or access readers, with their physical floor positions by using sound events detected during elevator operation or commissioning. The procedure relies on detected sound peaks, acoustic signatures, or frequency shifts that occur when the elevator car passes, stops, or interacts with a floor fixture location.

## Technical Description

An elevator system includes an elevator control, an elevator car movable in a hoistway, and a plurality of floor fixtures connected to the elevator control via a wired or wireless communication network. Each floor fixture is installed at a landing associated with a respective floor. The elevator car, the hoistway, or the fixtures include one or more acoustic sensors configured to detect sound signals generated during a learning run of the elevator car.

During the fixture position learning procedure, the elevator control causes the elevator car to travel through the hoistway according to a predefined learning sequence. While the car moves past the landings, the acoustic sensor records sound data. The recorded sound data is analyzed to identify characteristic sound peaks, impulse events, Doppler-related frequency shifts, resonance changes, or other acoustic features associated with the presence or activation of a floor fixture.

For example, a fixture may emit a short acoustic pulse, tone, click, relay sound, piezoelectric signal, or ultrasonic signal when commanded by the elevator control. Alternatively, the fixture may be passive and may generate a detectable acoustic reflection, resonance, or frequency shift as the elevator car passes its landing. The time at which the detected acoustic feature occurs is correlated with car position information obtained from an encoder, hoistway position sensor, door-zone sensor, speed profile, motor feedback, or other position reference. Based on this correlation, the elevator control determines the physical position of the fixture.

## Learning Sequence

The learning procedure may include the following steps:

1. **Initialization**  
   The elevator control enters a fixture learning mode. Existing fixture addresses are read from the communication bus, and each fixture is placed in a learning-ready state.

2. **Reference Positioning**  
   The elevator car is moved to a known reference position, such as the lowest landing, top landing, or a shaft reference switch. The elevator control initializes a car position reference.

3. **Commanded Acoustic Emission**  
   The elevator control individually commands each connected floor fixture to generate a predetermined acoustic signal. The signal may be audible or ultrasonic and may have a defined frequency, pulse pattern, duration, modulation, or amplitude.

4. **Car Movement and Detection**  
   The car is moved along the hoistway. An acoustic sensor mounted on the car, in the hoistway, or at selected landings detects sound signals. The detected signal is filtered and processed to identify sound peaks or frequency components matching the commanded fixture signal.

5. **Peak or Frequency-Shift Identification**  
   The elevator control or a signal processing unit determines the time or car position at which a sound peak, maximum sound pressure level, minimum propagation delay, maximum reflected intensity, or characteristic Doppler frequency shift occurs. This point corresponds to the closest approach of the car-mounted sensor to the emitting or reflecting fixture.

6. **Position Correlation**  
   The identified acoustic event is correlated with the elevator car position at the same time. The corresponding car position is assigned as the vertical position of the fixture.

7. **Fixture-to-Floor Assignment**  
   The determined fixture position is compared with known floor level positions or learned landing positions. The elevator control assigns the fixture address to the nearest floor or landing.

8. **Validation**  
   The procedure may be repeated in the opposite travel direction or at a different car speed. A valid assignment is accepted when repeated measurements are within a specified tolerance.

9. **Storage**  
   The learned association between fixture address and floor position is stored in non-volatile memory of the elevator control.

## Acoustic Signal Processing

The detected acoustic data may be processed using one or more of the following techniques:

- band-pass filtering around an expected fixture emission frequency;
- peak detection in a time-domain sound pressure signal;
- spectral analysis using FFT or short-time Fourier transform;
- correlation with a known emitted pulse pattern;
- Doppler shift analysis caused by relative motion between the car-mounted sensor and a stationary fixture;
- time-of-arrival or time-difference-of-arrival estimation;
- envelope detection to determine the point of maximum acoustic intensity;
- rejection of background noise caused by guide shoes, doors, ventilation, or motor operation.

In one implementation, the fixture emits a fixed-frequency tone while the elevator car passes the landing. The frequency detected by a moving car-mounted microphone shifts upward while the car approaches the fixture and downward after passing the fixture. The zero-crossing or inflection point of the Doppler shift, or the point at which the detected frequency equals the nominal emission frequency, indicates that the sensor is approximately adjacent to the fixture. The elevator control records the car position at that instant and assigns the fixture to the corresponding floor.

In another implementation, the fixture emits a short acoustic pulse when commanded. The detected sound pressure level increases as the car approaches the emitting fixture and decreases after passing it. The position corresponding to the maximum detected peak amplitude is used as the fixture location.

## Example Procedure

A car-mounted microphone is connected to the elevator control. Each landing fixture has a unique bus address and includes a small acoustic emitter. During commissioning, the control commands fixture address A1 to emit a 20 kHz tone. The elevator car travels upward at a constant low speed. The microphone detects the tone and the control calculates the received frequency over time. As the car approaches the fixture, the detected frequency is slightly higher than 20 kHz. After the car passes the fixture, the detected frequency becomes slightly lower than 20 kHz. The control determines the transition point between the positive and negative frequency shift and records the corresponding car encoder position. The recorded position is matched to the nearest landing level, and address A1 is stored as the fixture for that floor. The same process is repeated for all fixture addresses.

## Error Handling and Reliability

The procedure may include plausibility checks to improve reliability. If two fixtures are assigned to the same floor, the control may repeat the measurement using different tones or pulse patterns. If no peak or frequency shift is detected, the fixture may be flagged as missing, incorrectly connected, or acoustically obstructed. If the detected position lies outside an acceptable distance from any known floor level, the system may request manual confirmation or perform a second learning run.

The elevator control may compensate for car speed, acoustic propagation delay, microphone placement, hoistway temperature, and expected sound attenuation. Measurements from upward and downward runs may be averaged to reduce directional error. Multiple microphones may also be used to improve localization and to distinguish fixtures on opposite sides of the hoistway or at front and rear landings.

## Result

After completion of the learning procedure, the elevator control has a stored mapping between each connected floor fixture and its physical floor position. This mapping can be used for normal elevator operation, fixture diagnostics, automatic commissioning, replacement fixture identification, and detection of incorrectly wired or incorrectly addressed landing devices.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a patent abstract about identifying elevator floor fixtures by measuring sound propagation in the elevator shaft and correlating acoustic events with elevator car position.
counterfactuals.output: An elevator floor fixture identification system includes one or more acoustic sensors arranged in or on an elevator car, hoistway, or landing region to detect sound propagating within an elevator shaft. As the elevator car moves along the shaft, acoustic events generated by or reflected from floor-related fixtures, including landing doors, sill structures, buttons, indicator housings, brackets, rails, or other installation features, are measured and time-stamped. A controller determines elevator car position during the measurements and correlates detected acoustic signatures, time-of-flight characteristics, amplitude variations, Doppler effects, reverberation patterns, or spectral features with corresponding car positions. Based on the correlation, the controller identifies the presence, type, and location of floor fixtures at respective landings and may generate a fixture map of the elevator installation. The fixture map can be used for commissioning, maintenance, inspection, modernization planning, diagnostic comparison, or autonomous elevator operation.
